nameStory: Rough horsetail gets its name from its coarse, sandpapery texture that was once used to scour pots and sharpen tools - hence its other common name, scouring rush. The 'horsetail' part comes from the plant's resemblance to a horse's tail, with its long, segmented stems that look like they could swish flies away.
description: Rough horsetail is an ancient-looking plant that doesn't quite fit the typical idea of a fern, though it's related to them. It grows as tall, hollow, green stems that are distinctly segmented like bamboo, reaching knee to waist height. Unlike most plants, it has no leaves - just these striking, vertical green tubes topped with small cone-like structures. The stems are evergreen, staying green through winter when most other plants have died back.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctive hollow, jointed stems that feel remarkably rough and gritty to the touch, like natural sandpaper. The green stems are ridged lengthwise and have dark bands at each joint.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Grows in upright clumps of unbranched stems that look like green tubes or straws standing at attention. Each stem is perfectly straight and uniform in width.

idTips.label: Joints
idTips.description: Dark bands circle the stem at regular intervals where segments meet, creating a bamboo-like appearance. You can often pull the stem apart at these joints with a satisfying 'pop'.

idTips.label: Spore Cones
idTips.description: Small, pointed, cone-like structures appear at stem tips in spring and early summer. They're yellowish-brown and release clouds of spores when mature.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire stem feels incredibly rough and abrasive due to silica deposits in the plant tissue. Running your finger along it creates a distinctive scratchy sensation.

habitat: Look for rough horsetail in moist, sandy or gravelly areas like streambanks, pond edges, and wet meadows throughout New England. It particularly loves spots where the soil stays damp but not waterlogged, often growing alongside sedges and rushes. You'll also find it in disturbed wet areas like ditches and the edges of wetland trails.

seasonality.spring: Spore-bearing cones appear at stem tips, releasing yellowish clouds of spores when tapped. New stems emerge from underground rhizomes, initially appearing as small green tubes.
seasonality.summer: Stems reach full height and the distinctive rough texture is most noticeable. Cones may persist or fall off, leaving blunt stem tips.
seasonality.fall: Stems remain green and prominent while surrounding vegetation dies back, making the plant more conspicuous in the landscape.
seasonality.winter: One of the few 'fern relatives' that stays bright green through snow and freezing temperatures, creating striking vertical lines in winter wetlands.

funFact: This plant is essentially a living fossil - rough horsetail's ancestors grew as tall as trees 300 million years ago and dominated ancient forests alongside dinosaurs, but today's species are evolutionary 'bonsai' versions of those prehistoric giants.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other horsetails, but rough horsetail is the only one that's evergreen and completely unbranched. If you see branching stems or stems that die back in winter, you're looking at a different horsetail species. Remember: 'rough and simple' for this species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a horsetail, this plant is actually more closely related to ferns than to any flowering plant. It reproduces by spores rather than seeds and represents an ancient lineage that predates both flowers and cones.
compareHints: Rough horsetail stands apart from other New England horsetails by being evergreen and completely unbranched - other species like field horsetail have distinctive branching patterns and die back in winter. While meadow horsetail and wood horsetail create delicate, almost feathery appearances with their branches, rough horsetail maintains a stark, minimalist look year-round.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field horsetail is the most common horsetail in New England and differs from its relatives by having the most delicate, finely divided branches - rough horsetail has thick, unbranched stems, while wood horsetail has branches that branch again, creating a more feathery appearance.
Wood horsetail stands out from other New England horsetails by its distinctly twice-divided, lacy branching pattern that creates a soft, feathery appearance.

Dwarf horsetail stands out from all other New England horsetails simply by being dramatically smaller - while field horsetail might reach 2 feet and rough horsetail can tower at 4 feet, dwarf horsetail maxes out around one foot tall.
Among New England's horsetails, water horsetail is the wetland specialist with simple unbranched stems.
Variegated horsetail is much smaller and more delicate than rough horsetail, lacks the branching side shoots of field horsetail, and stays more compact than water horsetail.
Meadow horsetail stands out from other New England horsetails by its preference for shaded, moist areas and its distinctly delicate, feathery branching pattern.
Marsh horsetail differs from its common relative field horsetail by preferring wetter habitats and having more delicate, less robust branching.
